newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - No end in sight to German tax deadlock.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - No end in sight to German tax deadlock.

text.p: Germany all but abandoned its bid to reach compromise on tax reforms on Tuesday, opening the way for government and opposition to fight out the issue in an epic campaign ahead of general elections next year.

Both Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said they saw no chance of a deal in parliament's reconciliation process on government plans to slash income and corporate taxes.
"It has become clear that the SPD is on a confrontation course, and that above all it is living up to its name as a party of tax increases," Finance Minister Theo Waigel said.
"The SPD is not in the slightest bit interested in a serious tax reform," he told reporters.

Waigel was speaking after two days of informal negotiations with the SPD ahead of a meeting of parliament's mediation committee on Wednesday -- called after the SPD voted down his tax reforms in the Bundesrat upper house earlier this month.

Kohl's government had billed Waigel's plan to cut some 30 billion marks ($16.3 billion) in taxes as the 'reform of the century' which would boost investment and job creation in a country where the number of people out of work is near post-war highs.
Key elements included slashing the main rate of corporation tax to 35 percent from 47 percent by 1999 and cutting the top rate of income tax to 39 percent from 53 percent.
The SPD says the tax reform would benefit businesses and the rich at the expense of ordinary workers.
"It is clear that we will not support the tax reforms in the mediation committee because we consider them unjust and anti-social," SPD chief whip Peter Struck said after the talks.

Even an offer by the coalition to lighten the tax burden by just 15 billion marks was rejected by the SPD -- which instead has proposed cuts in occupational insurance charges to cut the cost of labour and shorten Germany's four-million dole queue.
Struck said he still held out hopes of agreeing to a cut in pensions and unemployment insurance charges by one percentage point each from this October.
But both Waigel and Hans-Peter Repnik, negotiator for Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), said they could not accept the SPD's proposal to hike petrol taxes to pay for the cuts.

And Labour Minister Norbert Bluem said the SPD's financing proposals for cutting pensions charges would only work in the short term and undermine a government pension reform bill now making its way through parliament.

Rejection of the tax reforms by the mediation committee will send the measures back to the Bundestag lower house of parliament, which will interrupt its summer recess to meet next Tuesday to debate the tax reforms.
There, the two sides are likely to trade the blame for the breakdown in Germany's consensus-based politics, opening the way for a marathon campaign ahead of general elections in September 1998.

SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine said the extra session amounted to "an election campaign show by Chancellor Kohl", and he urged a deal be reached to cut the labour insurance charges and scrap the capital trading tax.
"There must be an agreement," he told Wednesday's Express newspaper. "That would increase investment and relieve workers.
Coalition leaders said they did not rule out convening the mediation committee again to exhaust all options in the search for a tax deal.

"We will do all that is humanly possible...to defend our tax reform," Waigel said. "Even if the SPD rejects the tax reform in the mediation committee or in the Bundesrat it will stay on the agenda -- this year, next year and after the parliamentary elections."

Both sides said there were still hopes of ending a two-year row on abolishing a capital trading tax -- which companies must pay even when they make a loss and would have to be introduced in eastern Germany if no deal is reached to scrap it.
Differences remain, however, on how municipal governments could be compensated for a resulting loss in revenues.
"We may be able to reach agreement on abolishing the capital trading tax -- I have not given up hope," Waigel said. ($ = 1.836 German Marks)
